claims.claim: John of Damascus was a Christian monk, priest, hymnographer, and apologist who was born and raised in Damascus c. AD 675 or AD 676, and whose death is traditionally placed at his monastery, Mar Saba, near Jerusalem, on 4 December AD 749.
John of Damascus was given the by-name of Chrysorroas (Χρυσορρόας, literally 'streaming with gold', i.e. 'the golden speaker').
John of Damascus was ordained priest by Patriarch John V of Jerusalem shortly after entering the monastery of Mar Saba.
John of Damascus is one of the Fathers of the Eastern Orthodox Church and is best known for his strong defence of icons.
The Catholic Church regards John of Damascus as a Doctor of the Church, often referred to as the Doctor of the Assumption due to his writings on the Assumption of Mary.
The work 'Quid est homo' is titled in Greek 'Τί ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος;' (What is a human being?).
The work 'Quid est homo' is described in its manuscript heading as a letter (Ἐπιστολὴ) of John, priest of Damascus, sent to someone (πρός τινα πεμφθεῖσα).
The work 'Quid est homo' survives in Migne's Patrologia Graeca, volume 94, columns 244, and is catalogued with approximate dates 0675-0749 for the author.

The work 'Quid est homo' addresses the composition of the human body from four elements: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile, and associates different temperaments with the predominance of each humor.
In 'Quid est homo', John of Damascus states that the human being is 'a rational mortal animal, receptive of mind and knowledge' (ζῶον λογικὸν θνητὸν, νοῦ καὶ ἐπιστήμης δεκτικόν).
The work 'Quid est homo' discusses the brain as the source of the senses and the location of the soul and the depth of thoughts, with power and prudence sent up from the liver to the brain.
